analysis.investment_thesis: Delhivery is a venture-capital-style bet dressed as a listed stock — it generated its first meaningful profit (INR 162 Cr) only in FY25 after losing INR 4,736 Cr cumulatively over the prior six years, yet trades at 192x trailing earnings. There is no promoter, no pricing power, no durable moat, and the business model depends entirely on e-commerce volumes that could be internalised by platform players at any time.
key_strengths: Revenue growing at 32.5% CAGR — scale is being built and market share is real
Low D/E of 0.17 — the balance sheet is not the primary concern
OCF turned consistently positive in FY24-FY25, suggesting operating leverage is beginning to work
key_risks: ROE of 1.52% and ROCE of 2.47% — the business is destroying value in real terms relative to cost of capital
Operating margin of 0.79% leaves zero buffer for any volume or pricing shock
Existential dependence on Meesho, Flipkart, Amazon — any in-house logistics push by these customers ends the growth story
red_flags: No promoter holding whatsoever — this is an institutional speculation, not an owner-operated business
Six consecutive years of net losses totalling over INR 4,700 Cr; one year of thin profitability does not establish a franchise
P/E of 192x for a barely-profitable logistics company competing on price is completely disconnected from any reasonable valuation
analysis.detailed_analysis:
I built DMart by understanding that retail is a low-margin, operationally intensive business where every paisa of cost matters. Delhivery operates in an even harsher environment — third-party logistics, where the customer can switch providers or build in-house, and where margins are structurally thin. An operating margin of 0.79% on INR 8,932 Cr of revenue means INR 71 Cr of operating profit — one bad quarter erases that entirely. The 'other income' of INR 442 Cr (largely interest on cash) is larger than operating income, which tells me the business model itself is not yet viable.

More fundamentally, I only invest in businesses where I understand who will be the owner ten years from now and why they will still be protecting the franchise. With no promoter, 48.6% FII ownership, and a business dependent on e-commerce platform goodwill, I have no such confidence. The 32.5% revenue CAGR is a venture story, not an investment story. I will not own this.
